units.title: Module 1: Properties of Multiplication and Division and Solving Problems with Units of 2–5 and 10
units.subtitle: Equal Groups, Arrays, Unknown Factors, Commutative & Distributive Properties
units.overview: This 22-day module builds on fluency with addition and arrays to develop conceptual understanding of multiplication and division with units of 2–5 and 10, exploring equal groups, arrays, strip diagrams, and the commutative and distributive properties.
learningObjectives: Understand equal groups of objects as multiplication and write multiplication equations using arrays.
Understand division as an unknown factor problem (size of group or number of groups).
Demonstrate the commutativity of multiplication and model the distributive property to decompose units.
Solve one- and two-step word problems involving multiplication and division within 100 using Read-Draw-Write (RDW).

vocabulary.definition: A rectangular arrangement of equal groups organized in rows and columns.
vocabulary.exampleSentence: A 3 by 5 array has 3 rows with 5 tiles in each row.

vocabulary.definition: Changing the order of the factors in a multiplication equation does not change its product.
vocabulary.exampleSentence: By the commutative property, 3 × 5 = 5 × 3 = 15.

vocabulary.definition: To multiply each part of a decomposed factor by the other factor.
vocabulary.exampleSentence: We can distribute 7 × 4 as (5 × 4) + (2 × 4).

vocabulary.definition: The numbers multiplied together in a multiplication expression or equation.
vocabulary.exampleSentence: In 4 × 3 = 12, the numbers 4 and 3 are the factors.

vocabulary.definition: The total when multiplying two or more numbers together.
vocabulary.exampleSentence: The product of 4 and 5 is 20.

vocabulary.definition: The number resulting from the division of two numbers.
vocabulary.exampleSentence: In 18 ÷ 3 = 6, the quotient is 6.

vocabulary.definition: A rectangular model that looks like a segment of tape used to show number relationships.
vocabulary.exampleSentence: Draw a strip diagram with 4 equal units to solve the division word problem.

units.title: Module 2: Place Value and Problem Solving with Units of Measure
units.subtitle: Time Intervals, Weight, Liquid Volume, Place Value to 100,000, Rounding & Standard Algorithm
units.overview: Students explore measurements of time intervals in minutes, weight in ounces and pounds, liquid volume in liters, milliliters, and customary units, extend place value understanding up to 100,000, round numbers on a vertical number line, and add/subtract within 1,000 using the standard algorithm.
learningObjectives: Solve problems involving addition and subtraction of time intervals in minutes on a number line and clock.
Determine weight (oz, lb) and liquid volume (mL, L, cups, pints, quarts, gallons) using appropriate units and tools.
Compose, decompose, read, write, compare (<, >, =), and order numbers up to 100,000 including expanded notation.
Round whole numbers on a vertical number line and fluently add and subtract within 1,000 using the standard algorithm.

vocabulary.definition: An equation that is a sum of multiplication expressions, each representing the value of one digit as the product of that digit and a place value unit.
The distance or time elapsed between two points on a number line.
vocabulary.exampleSentence: The time interval from 2:15 p.m. to 2:45 p.m. is 30 minutes.

vocabulary.definition: A measurement of the amount of space that liquid takes up in a container.
vocabulary.exampleSentence: We measured the liquid volume of water in the beaker in milliliters.

vocabulary.definition: Numbers that make mental calculations more efficient when estimating solutions.
vocabulary.exampleSentence: To estimate 28 + 37, we can use compatible numbers or round to 30 + 40 = 70.

vocabulary.definition: A systematic process for adding or subtracting numbers one place value unit at a time.
vocabulary.exampleSentence: Use the standard algorithm to regroup 10 ones as 1 ten.

units.title: Module 3: Multiplication and Division with Units of 0, 1, 6–9, and Multiples of 10
units.subtitle: Multiplicative Comparison, Input-Output Tables, Associative Property & Two-Digit by One-Digit Multiplication
units.overview: Students explore multiplicative comparison, input-output tables, multiplication and division with units of 0, 1, 6, 7, 8, and 9, even/odd divisibility by 2, multiplying by multiples of 10, and multiplying two-digit numbers by one-digit numbers using area models and the standard algorithm.
learningObjectives: Describe multiplication as a comparison (e.g., 3 × 24 represents 3 times as much as 24) and represent number pairs in input-output tables.
Recall and apply multiplication and division facts for 0, 1, 6, 7, 8, and 9 using distributive and associative properties.
Determine if a number is even or odd using the divisibility rule for 2.
Multiply a two-digit number by a one-digit number using place value disks, area models, partial products, and the standard algorithm.

vocabulary.definition: A model for multiplication problems that relates a rectangular array to the area of a rectangle.
vocabulary.exampleSentence: We decomposed 24 × 3 into (20 × 3) + (4 × 3) using an area model.

vocabulary.definition: A table with inputs in the first column/row and corresponding outputs following a rule in the second column/row.
vocabulary.exampleSentence: In the input-output table, each input is multiplied by 6 to get the output.

vocabulary.definition: The product of a given number and another whole number found when skip-counting.
vocabulary.exampleSentence: The numbers 6, 12, 18, and 24 are multiples of 6.

vocabulary.definition: One of the products resulting from decomposing one factor and multiplying each part by the other factor.
vocabulary.exampleSentence: For 14 × 3, the partial products are 30 and 12, which add to 42.

vocabulary.definition: Capable of being evenly partitioned into equal groups with zero remainder.
vocabulary.exampleSentence: Every even number is divisible by 2.

units.title: Module 4: Multiplication and Area
units.subtitle: Unit Squares, Rectangular Arrays, Area Formula & Additive Property of Composite Figures
units.overview: Students explore area as an attribute of two-dimensional figures, tiling rectangles with unit squares without gaps or overlaps, connecting rows × unit squares per row to multiplication, and decomposing composite figures into non-overlapping rectangles.
learningObjectives: Determine the area of rectangles with whole-number side lengths using multiplication (rows × unit squares in each row).
Find an unknown side length when given the area and one side length of a rectangle.
Decompose composite figures formed by rectangles into non-overlapping rectangles to find total area.

vocabulary.definition: The measurement attribute that describes the number of unit squares a figure or region covers.
vocabulary.exampleSentence: A rectangle with 4 rows of 6 square centimeters has an area of 24 square centimeters.

vocabulary.definition: A unit of area in the shape of a square that has side lengths of 1 unit.
vocabulary.exampleSentence: We measured the area in square inches and square centimeters.

vocabulary.definition: To cover a region with unit squares without gaps or overlaps.
vocabulary.exampleSentence: Tile the rectangle with 15 square inch tiles.

units.title: Module 5: Fractions as Numbers on the Number Line
units.subtitle: Unit Fractions, Partitioning Wholes, Number Line Distances, Equivalent Fractions & Comparing Fractions
units.overview: Students transition from understanding fractions as equal parts of a shape to understanding fractions as points and distances on a number line, composing non-unit fractions from unit fractions, finding equivalent fractions, and comparing fractions with like numerators or like denominators.
learningObjectives: Partition wholes into equal parts (halves, thirds, fourths, sixths, eighths) and compose fractions as a sum of unit fractions.
Locate and represent fractions between 0 and 1 on a number line, including halves, fourths, and eighths.
Determine and explain equivalent fractions using visual models and the same point on a number line.
Compare two fractions having the same numerator or same denominator using <, >, or = and justify with models.

vocabulary.definition: A fraction with a numerator of 1 that represents one equal part of a whole (e.g., 1/2, 1/3, 1/4, 1/6, 1/8).
vocabulary.exampleSentence: The fraction 3/4 is composed of three copies of the unit fraction 1/4.

vocabulary.definition: Fractions that name the same size of a same-size whole or the exact same point on a number line.
vocabulary.exampleSentence: 1/2 and 2/4 are equivalent fractions because they land on the same point on the number line.

vocabulary.definition: A unit created by partitioning a whole into a number of equal parts (halves, thirds, fourths, sixths, eighths).
vocabulary.exampleSentence: When a strip is folded into 8 equal parts, the fractional unit is eighths.

vocabulary.definition: To divide a whole shape or number line interval into equal parts.
vocabulary.exampleSentence: Partition the number line from 0 to 1 into 6 equal parts to show sixths.

units.title: Module 6: Financial Literacy and Data
units.subtitle: Coins & Bills, Human Capital, Scarcity, Saving & Credit, Frequency Tables, Scaled Graphs & Dot Plots
units.overview: Students count collections of coins and bills, explore human capital and income, supply/scarcity and cost, planned/unplanned spending, saving, credit and interest, and represent and solve one- and two-step problems using frequency tables, scaled pictographs, scaled bar graphs, and dot plots.
learningObjectives: Determine the value of a collection of coins and bills.
Explain human capital/labor and income, resource scarcity and cost, saving, credit, borrower responsibility, and interest.
Create and analyze frequency tables, scaled bar graphs, pictographs, and dot plots to solve one- and two-step problems.
Represent real-world relationships using number pairs in a table.

vocabulary.definition: Buying or obtaining goods and services now with an agreement to pay in the future.
vocabulary.exampleSentence: When you use credit, the borrower must pay the lender back, usually with interest.

vocabulary.definition: Extra money paid for borrowing money or making purchases on credit.
vocabulary.exampleSentence: Paying back a loan with interest costs more than the original price.

vocabulary.definition: A graph that represents data along a horizontal line where each value is shown by a dot in a vertical column.
vocabulary.exampleSentence: The dot plot shows that 89 prizes was the most frequent score.

vocabulary.definition: A table that lists categories or items and shows the number of times each occurs.
vocabulary.exampleSentence: We organized the class survey results into a frequency table.

vocabulary.definition: A bar graph or pictograph with a scale that uses units greater than 1.
vocabulary.exampleSentence: In this scaled bar graph, each grid line represents 5 students.

units.title: Module 7: Geometry and Measurement Word Problems
units.subtitle: 2D Polygons & Quadrilaterals, 3D Solids, Perimeter, Missing Side Lengths & Area vs. Perimeter
units.overview: Students classify and sort 2D polygons (especially quadrilaterals: rhombuses, parallelograms, trapezoids, rectangles, squares) and 3D solids (cones, cylinders, spheres, prisms, cubes), calculate perimeter and unknown side lengths, and solve multi-operation word problems comparing area and perimeter.
learningObjectives: Classify and sort 2D polygons and 3D solids (cones, cylinders, spheres, triangular and rectangular prisms, cubes) by attributes (faces, edges, vertices).
Recognize rhombuses, parallelograms, trapezoids, rectangles, and squares as subcategories of quadrilaterals.
Determine the perimeter of a polygon or a missing side length when given the perimeter and remaining side lengths.
Solve one- and two-step word problems involving area, perimeter, and all four operations.

vocabulary.definition: The boundary or total length around the boundary of a two-dimensional shape.
vocabulary.exampleSentence: A rectangle with side lengths 4 cm and 2 cm has a perimeter of 4 + 2 + 4 + 2 = 12 cm.

vocabulary.definition: A polygon with all equal side lengths and equal interior angles.
vocabulary.exampleSentence: A regular hexagon with a perimeter of 24 inches has 6 sides of 4 inches each.

vocabulary.definition: A four-sided polygon with four angles, including trapezoids, parallelograms, rectangles, rhombuses, and squares.
vocabulary.exampleSentence: Every square is a rectangle, a rhombus, a parallelogram, and a quadrilateral.

vocabulary.definition: A face is a flat 2D surface of a 3D solid; an edge is the line segment where two faces meet.
vocabulary.exampleSentence: A triangular prism has 5 faces, 9 edges, and 6 vertices.

units.title: Unit 1: Classic Tales: The Wind in the Willows
units.subtitle: Literary Elements, Character Analysis, Plot Sequencing, Themes, Point of View & Opinion Writing
units.overview: Students listen to and analyze Kenneth Grahame's classic tale The Wind in the Willows alongside Reader selections 'Aladdin and the Wonderful Lamp' and 'Alice's Adventures in Wonderland,' exploring personification, perspective, plot sequence, character traits, and themes of friendship, loyalty, hospitality, and responsibility.
learningObjectives: Analyze characters' internal and external traits, motivations, and relationships (Mole, Water Rat, Badger, Mr. Toad).
Identify and sequence plot elements (rising action, climax, falling action, resolution) and setting.
Explain literary themes of friendship, loyalty, hospitality, and responsibility using text evidence.
Identify point of view (first-person vs. third-person) and personification, and write an opinion paragraph.

vocabulary.definition: Wandered or wound slowly and gently without a straight path.
vocabulary.exampleSentence: The river meandered peacefully through the green English countryside.

vocabulary.definition: Sad, low-spirited, and discouraged.
vocabulary.exampleSentence: Mole felt dejected after the boat overturned in the cold river.

vocabulary.definition: Called upon or gathered courage or someone to come.
vocabulary.exampleSentence: Rat summoned his courage and knocked on Mr. Badger's door.

vocabulary.definition: Expressed disappointment or disapproval toward someone for their actions.
vocabulary.exampleSentence: Rat reproached Mole for wandering into the Wild Wood alone.

vocabulary.definition: Having an excessively high opinion of oneself; vain and boastful.
vocabulary.exampleSentence: Mr. Toad was conceited and bragged constantly about how clever he was.

vocabulary.definition: Acting carelessly without thinking or caring about danger or consequences.
vocabulary.exampleSentence: Toad drove the motorcar recklessly down the country lane.

assessments: Beginning-of-Year (BOY) Silent Reading & Word Reading Assessment (Lessons 6–10)
units.readerTitle: Classic Tales (The Wind in the Willows, Aladdin, Alice in Wonderland)

units.title: Unit 2: Scales, Feathers, and Fur: Animal Classification
units.subtitle: Informational Text Features, Central Idea, Vertebrates vs. Invertebrates & Text Structures
units.overview: Guided by narrator Rattenborough, students read informational texts classifying animals into vertebrates and invertebrates, warm-blooded and cold-blooded organisms, and the five vertebrate groups: fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds, and mammals.
learningObjectives: Use text features (headings, captions, diagrams, bold print, glossaries) to locate information in informational texts.
Determine the central idea and supporting details about vertebrate and invertebrate animal groups.
Compare and contrast warm-blooded and cold-blooded animals and explain how scientists classify living things.
Identify prefixes (un-, non-, re-, pre-) and root words, and compose an informational paragraph.

vocabulary.definition: An animal that has a backbone (spinal column).
vocabulary.exampleSentence: Fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds, and mammals are all vertebrates.

vocabulary.definition: An animal that does not have a backbone.
vocabulary.exampleSentence: Insects, spiders, and jellyfish are invertebrates.

vocabulary.definition: A complete change of physical form or structure during an animal's life cycle.
vocabulary.exampleSentence: Tadpoles undergo metamorphosis as they grow legs and lungs to become adult frogs.

vocabulary.definition: Living or growing in or near water.
vocabulary.exampleSentence: Fish are aquatic animals that breathe oxygen through gills.

assessments: Unit 2 Reading Comprehension & Informational Writing Assessment (Lesson 15)

units.title: Unit 3: The Human Body: Systems and Senses
units.subtitle: Skeletal, Muscular, and Nervous Systems, Sight & Hearing, Context Clues & Explanatory Writing
units.overview: Dr. Welbody introduces students to the interconnected systems of the human body—the skeletal system, muscular system, nervous system, and the senses of vision and hearing—while practicing topic sentences, concluding sentences, and regular/irregular plural nouns.
learningObjectives: Explain how the skeletal, muscular, and nervous systems work together to allow the human body to move and think.
Describe how the parts of the eye and ear function to provide vision and hearing.
Synthesize details across paragraphs to retell and paraphrase informational texts.
Decode and use prefixes dis- and mis- and write well-structured explanatory paragraphs.

vocabulary.definition: Done by choice; controlled consciously by a person's brain.
vocabulary.exampleSentence: Bicep muscles are voluntary muscles because you choose when to bend your arm.

vocabulary.definition: Happening automatically without conscious control.
vocabulary.exampleSentence: Your heart beating is controlled by involuntary cardiac muscle.

vocabulary.definition: Strong, flexible tissue that cushions bones at joints and shapes the nose and ears.
vocabulary.exampleSentence: Cartilage keeps your bones from rubbing together at your knees.

vocabulary.definition: Special nerve cells that receive signals from light, sound, or touch and send messages to the brain.
vocabulary.exampleSentence: Sensory receptors in your skin alert your brain when something is hot.

assessments: Unit 3 Assessment: The Human Body Systems & Senses (Lesson 13)

units.title: Unit 4: The Ancient Roman Civilization
units.subtitle: Roman Mythology, Republic to Empire, Julius & Augustus Caesar, Literary Myths vs. Historical Nonfiction
units.overview: Students explore the rise and legacy of Ancient Rome—from the legend of Romulus and Remus and Roman mythology to the Roman Republic, Julius Caesar, Augustus Caesar, Roman architecture (aqueducts, Colosseum, Pantheon), and the decline of the Empire.
learningObjectives: Distinguish between historical nonfiction and traditional Roman myths and legends.
Analyze historical figures (Julius Caesar, Augustus, Cleopatra, Constantine) and their impact on Roman history.
Use suffixes (-y, -al, -ist, -ian) and past/present/future verb tenses accurately.
Write a persuasive/argumentative opinion essay supported by historical text evidence.

vocabulary.definition: A form of government in which citizens elect representatives to make laws and vote.
vocabulary.exampleSentence: Before emperors ruled, Ancient Rome was governed as a republic by the Senate.

vocabulary.definition: Wealthy, noble upper-class ruling families in Ancient Rome.
vocabulary.exampleSentence: Patricians held the highest positions in the early Roman Senate.

vocabulary.definition: Ordinary working citizens and farmers of Ancient Rome.
vocabulary.exampleSentence: Plebeians worked hard to gain a voice and fair laws in the Roman government.

vocabulary.definition: A bridge-like stone channel built by Romans to carry fresh water from distant hills into cities.
vocabulary.exampleSentence: Roman engineers constructed stone aqueducts that stood for centuries.

units.title: Unit 5: Flash, Bang, Boom! Exploring Light and Sound
units.subtitle: Reflection, Refraction, Lenses, Color Spectrum, Sound Vibrations, Pitch/Volume & Research Newspaper Article
units.overview: Students investigate the physics of light (wavelengths, reflection, mirrors, refraction, concave/convex lenses, prisms) and sound (vibrations, sound waves, pitch, intensity, human voice) plus biographies of Alexander Graham Bell and Thomas Edison, culminating in writing a newspaper article.
learningObjectives: Explain cause-and-effect relationships in scientific texts about reflection, refraction, and sound vibrations.
Use graphic features and diagrams to understand how light travels through lenses and how sound travels through mediums.
Use suffixes -ous and -ly and conjunctions (and, but, because, so) to connect ideas.
Research and write an informative newspaper article about an invention (telephone or incandescent lightbulb).

vocabulary.definition: The bending of a light wave when it passes from one transparent medium into another, such as air into water.
vocabulary.exampleSentence: Refraction makes a straw in a glass of water look bent.

vocabulary.definition: Not allowing light to pass through, creating a shadow.
vocabulary.exampleSentence: A wooden door is opaque because no light can shine through it.

vocabulary.definition: Allowing light to pass through clearly so objects behind can be distinctly seen.
vocabulary.exampleSentence: Clear window glass is transparent.

vocabulary.definition: A rapid back-and-forth movement that creates sound waves.
vocabulary.exampleSentence: Plucking a guitar string causes a vibration that travels through the air to your ear.

assessments: Unit 5 Assessment & Newspaper Article Research Rubric (Lessons 14–16)

units.title: Unit 6: Astronomy: Our Solar System and Beyond
units.subtitle: Inner & Outer Planets, Asteroids/Comets/Meteors, Galaxies, Gravity, Copernicus, Mae Jemison & Informative Essay
units.overview: Students journey across our solar system and universe—studying the Sun, inner rocky planets, outer gas giants, asteroids, meteors, comets, stars, constellations, galaxies (Milky Way, Andromeda), gravity, Nicolaus Copernicus, the Space Shuttle, and astronaut Mae Jemison.
learningObjectives: Compare and contrast inner planets and outer planets, and distinguish between asteroids, meteoroids, meteors, and comets.
Analyze the structure of drama/Reader's Theater in the play about Nicolaus Copernicus.
Explain how gravity holds planets in orbit around the Sun and moons in orbit around planets.
Use suffixes -ful and -less and quotation marks, and write a multi-paragraph informative essay.

vocabulary.definition: The invisible force of attraction that pulls objects with mass toward one another.
vocabulary.exampleSentence: The Sun's strong gravity keeps Earth and the other planets in orbit.

vocabulary.definition: A massive system of billions of stars, gas, and dust held together by gravity.
vocabulary.exampleSentence: Our solar system is located in the Milky Way galaxy.

vocabulary.definition: An astronomical event where one celestial body moves into the shadow of another.
vocabulary.exampleSentence: During a solar eclipse, the Moon passes directly between Earth and the Sun.

vocabulary.definition: An idea or explanation that can be tested through observation and investigation.
vocabulary.exampleSentence: Copernicus formed the heliocentric hypothesis that Earth orbits the Sun.

assessments: Middle-of-Year (MOY) Benchmark Assessment & Unit 6 Informative Essay

units.title: Unit 7: Learning from the Land: Native American Regions and Cultures
units.subtitle: Beringia Migration, Mississippi Mound Builders, Southwest/Pueblo, Northeast, Caddo & Tejas of Texas, Arctic
units.overview: Students explore how Native American peoples adapted to diverse geographic regions across North America—including the Mississippi River Mound Builders, Pueblo peoples of the Southwest, the Caddo and Tejas nations of Texas, Eastern Woodland tribes, and Inuit peoples of the Arctic—through historical narratives and informational texts.
learningObjectives: Explain cause-and-effect relationships between geographic environments and Native American shelter, food, and culture.
Analyze fictional historical narratives ('Akando and Aponi', 'Alemeda, the Basket Weaver', 'Adoette and Awan') alongside informational chapters.
Apply suffixes -able and -ible and possessive nouns/pronouns.
Compare cultural traditions, including the Texas folktale 'Texas Paintbrush'.

vocabulary.definition: Moving from place to place in search of food and water rather than living in one permanent settlement.
vocabulary.exampleSentence: Early mammoth hunters lived a nomadic life following animal herds.

vocabulary.definition: Sun-dried bricks made of clay, mud, and straw used for building homes in the Southwest.
vocabulary.exampleSentence: Pueblo homes built of thick adobe stayed cool during hot desert afternoons.

vocabulary.definition: An alliance or league of groups or tribes united for mutual support and peace.
vocabulary.exampleSentence: The Caddo confederacy in East Texas was known as the Hasinai, meaning 'our own folk.'

assessments: Unit 7 Assessment: Native American Regions and Cultures (Lesson 13)

units.title: Unit 8: Travelers from Other Lands: Early Explorations of North America
units.subtitle: Columbus, Ponce de León, De Soto, Coronado in Texas/Southwest, Cabot, Hudson & Champlain
units.overview: Students study the motivations, voyages, challenges, and consequences of European exploration of North America—from Christopher Columbus, Juan Ponce de León, Hernando de Soto, and Francisco Vásquez de Coronado in the Southwest/Texas to John Cabot, Henry Hudson, and Samuel de Champlain in the search for the Northwest Passage.
learningObjectives: Identify the motivations (spice trade, gold, Northwest Passage, colonization) and routes of early European explorers.
Compare multiple perspectives of exploration, including impacts on Native American populations.
Use prefixes pro-, anti-, uni-, bi-, tri- and linking words (for example, in conclusion, furthermore).
Write a structured opinion essay evaluating explorer achievements and challenges.

vocabulary.definition: A journey undertaken by a group of people with a specific purpose, especially exploration.
vocabulary.exampleSentence: Coronado led a large expedition across the American Southwest and the Texas Panhandle.

vocabulary.definition: The science of planning and directing the course of a ship using maps, compasses, and stars.
vocabulary.exampleSentence: Sailors used an astrolabe and compass for ocean navigation.

vocabulary.definition: An open rebellion by sailors against the captain of a ship.
vocabulary.exampleSentence: Henry Hudson's crew staged a mutiny in the icy waters of Hudson Bay.

assessments: Unit 8 Assessment: Early Explorations of North America (Lesson 14)

units.title: Unit 9: Colonial America
units.subtitle: Roanoke, Jamestown, Plymouth/Mayflower Compact, New England, Middle & Southern Colonies, Road to Revolution
units.overview: Students trace the founding and daily life of the Thirteen English Colonies across the Southern, New England, and Middle regions—including Roanoke, Jamestown, Plymouth, the Massachusetts Bay Colony, William Penn and the Quakers, colonial trades, and the events leading toward the American Revolution.
learningObjectives: Compare and contrast geography, climate, economy, and daily life across the Southern, New England, and Middle Colonies.
Analyze historical narratives from the perspectives of colonial children alongside informational history chapters.
Apply prefixes im-, in-, non- and comparative/superlative adjectives (-er, -est, more, most).
Write a narrative story set in Colonial America using dialogue and descriptive details.

vocabulary.definition: A region settled and ruled by people from a distant country.
vocabulary.exampleSentence: Jamestown became the first permanent English colony in North America in 1607.

vocabulary.definition: The ability of citizens in a community to make their own laws and govern themselves.
vocabulary.exampleSentence: The Mayflower Compact was an early agreement for self-government.

vocabulary.definition: A young person who learns a skilled trade or craft by working for a master craftsman.
vocabulary.exampleSentence: The printer's apprentice learned how to set metal type for the colonial newspaper.

vocabulary.definition: To refuse to buy or use certain goods as a protest.
vocabulary.exampleSentence: Colonists organized a boycott of British tea to protest unfair taxes.

units.title: Unit 10: All That Jazz (Research Unit)
units.subtitle: Jazz Roots, Harlem Renaissance, Louis Armstrong, Billie Holiday, Tito Puente, Duke Ellington & Research Essay
units.overview: Students explore the vibrant music, poetry, and history of the Jazz Age and Harlem Renaissance—studying Louis Armstrong, Billie Holiday, Langston Hughes, Benny Goodman, Teddy Wilson, Tito Puente, and Duke Ellington—while conducting formal inquiry and research to write and present a biography essay with Works Cited.
learningObjectives: Generate research questions, distinguish primary and secondary sources, and cite reliable sources in a Works Cited list.
Evaluate details across biographies and informational texts to determine key ideas and author's voice.
Paraphrase information in one's own words to avoid plagiarism.
Compose, revise, edit, and present a research essay about a celebrated jazz musician.

vocabulary.definition: Creating and performing music spontaneously in the moment without written sheet music.
vocabulary.exampleSentence: Louis Armstrong was famous for his joyful trumpet improvisation.

vocabulary.definition: A rebirth or lively revival of art, literature, music, and learning.
vocabulary.exampleSentence: The Harlem Renaissance celebrated African American music, poetry, and visual art.

vocabulary.definition: Melody is the main tune of a song; harmony is the combination of musical notes played together to support the melody.
vocabulary.exampleSentence: The jazz band blended brass harmony with a swinging piano melody.

assessments: Grade 3 End-of-Year (EOY) Assessment & Research Essay / Presentation Rubric
units.readerTitle: All That Jazz Trade Books & Research Texts

units.title: Foundational Skills 1: Consonant Digraphs, Trigraphs & Syllable Division (VC/CV, VC/V, VCCCV)
units.subtitle: Digraphs (wh, sh, th, ng, nk, ck, ch/tch, dge/ge, ph/gh, kn/gn), Trigraphs (igh, ear, air, are) & Closed Syllables
units.overview: Students review and master consonant digraphs and trigraphs (wh, sh, th, ng, nk, ck, ch, tch, dge, ge, ph, gh, kn, gn, igh, ear, eer, ere, ore, air, are) and apply VC/CV, VC/V, and VCCCV syllable division rules to decode and encode multisyllabic words while reading Campfire Tales.
learningObjectives: Decode and spell words with common and advanced consonant digraphs and trigraphs (tch, dge, ph, gh, kn, gn, igh, ear, air).
Divide multisyllabic words into syllables using VC/CV, VC/V, and VCCCV patterns.
Read grade-level decodable texts (Campfire Tales) with accuracy, automaticity, and prosody.

vocabulary.definition: Two letters that work together to make a single sound (such as sh, ch, ph, kn).
vocabulary.exampleSentence: In the word 'phone', the digraph ph makes the /f/ sound.
vocabulary.phonicsPattern: wh, sh, th, ck, ch, ph, kn, gn

vocabulary.definition: Three letters that work together to represent a single sound (such as tch, dge, igh, ear).
vocabulary.exampleSentence: In the word 'bridge', the trigraph dge makes the /j/ sound after a short vowel.
vocabulary.phonicsPattern: tch, dge, igh, ear, air, are

examples.title: Read–Draw–Write: Equal Groups to Multiplication
examples.problem: Caroline, Brian, and Marta share a box of chocolates. They each get 4 chocolates. How many chocolates are there in all?
steps: Step 1 (Read): There are 3 friends (groups), and each friend gets 4 chocolates (size of each group).

Step 3 (Write Repeated Addition): 4 + 4 + 4 = 12.
Step 4 (Write Multiplication Equation): 3 groups of four = 3 × 4 = 12 chocolates.

examples.title: Comparing Unit Fractions (Course Guide & Module 5 Topic C)
examples.problem: Which fraction is greater: 1/6 or 1/8? Explain how you know.
steps: Step 1 (Compare Wholes): Draw two identical rectangles or number lines from 0 to 1.
Step 2 (Partition): Partition the first whole into 6 equal parts (sixths) and the second whole into 8 equal parts (eighths).
Step 3 (Reason About Size): The more equal parts a whole is partitioned into, the smaller each part is.
Step 4 (Compare): One sixth is larger than one eighth, so 1/6 > 1/8.
examples.solution: 1/6 > 1/8 because sixths are larger parts than eighths.

examples.title: Finding an Unknown Side Length from Perimeter
examples.problem: A rectangular bulletin board has a perimeter of 28 feet. Its top side length is 8 feet. What is its width?
steps: Step 1 (Opposite Sides of a Rectangle): Since the top is 8 feet, the bottom side is also 8 feet (8 + 8 = 16 feet).
Step 2 (Subtract from Perimeter): Subtract 16 feet from the total perimeter: 28 - 16 = 12 feet remaining for the left and right sides.
Step 3 (Divide by 2 Equal Widths): 12 ÷ 2 = 6 feet.
examples.solution: The width is 6 feet.

readingPassage.title: The River Bank, Part I (from The Wind in the Willows)
paragraphs: The Wind in the Willows follows the adventures of animals who live in the English countryside and act like people—a literary device called personification.

The chapter 'The River Bank' begins with Mole doing his spring cleaning. He has swept and dusted his underground tunnel. Suddenly, he smells the fresh spring air outside. He drops his paint brush, scrambles up the tunnel, and skips happily across the warm meadow until he reaches a glistening river full to the brim.

As Mole sits on the grassy bank watching the water meander by, a friendly Water Rat appears from a hole in the riverbank. Rat warmly invites Mole for his very first boat ride! Rat packs a generous picnic basket with cold chicken, crusty bread, and lemonade, and the two new friends float peacefully down the river together.

readingPassage.title: Meet Rattenborough & Classifying Vertebrates
readingPassage.authorOrSource: Rattenborough's Guide to Animals • Bluebonnet Grade 3 Unit 2
paragraphs: Greetings! Rattenborough, the famous explorer and animal expert, here! Scientists classify—or sort—animals into groups based on shared characteristics so we can understand how living things are related.

One of the most important ways taxonomists classify animals is by asking: Does this animal have a backbone? Animals with a backbone are called vertebrates. Animals without a backbone, such as insects, spiders, crabs, and jellyfish, are called invertebrates. In fact, more than 95 percent of all animal species on Earth are invertebrates!

Scientists further classify vertebrates into five main groups: fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds, and mammals. Fish, amphibians, and reptiles are cold-blooded—their body temperature changes with their surroundings. Birds and mammals are warm-blooded—their bodies maintain a constant internal temperature whether it is snowy or hot outside!
readingPassage.audioSummary: Read Rattenborough's explanation of how scientists classify animals into vertebrates and invertebrates.

readingPassage.title: How Do Your Skeleton, Joints, and Muscles Help You Move?
paragraphs: Your skeletal system is made up of more than 200 bones that give your body its strong shape and protect vital organs. Your skull protects your brain like a helmet, and your rib cage shields your heart and lungs.

Where two bones meet is called a joint. Strong elastic bands called ligaments hold bones together at joints, while smooth, flexible cartilage cushions the bones so they do not grind against each other.

Bones cannot move by themselves! Skeletal muscles are attached to bones by tough cords called tendons. When your brain sends an electrical message through your nervous system, voluntary muscles contract and pull on your bones so you can run, jump, and write!
readingPassage.audioSummary: Learn how the skeletal, muscular, and nervous systems team up to help you move.

readingPassage.title: Rome, Then and Now & The Pantheon
readingPassage.authorOrSource: Stories of Ancient Rome • Bluebonnet Grade 3 Unit 4
paragraphs: Over two thousand years ago, Rome grew from a small village along the Tiber River in Italy into one of the greatest civilizations in history. After overthrowing their kings, Romans established a republic—a government where citizens elected senators and consuls to represent them.
In the early Roman Republic, wealthy patricians held the most power, while ordinary working citizens, called plebeians, had very few rights until they united to demand fair written laws.

Romans were master builders and engineers. They constructed stone aqueducts to carry fresh water across valleys into cities, paved thousands of miles of roads, and built magnificent domes like the Pantheon, which still stands in Rome today with an open oculus at the top!

readingPassage.title: What Is Light, Refraction, and Sound?
readingPassage.authorOrSource: Adventures in Light and Sound • Bluebonnet Grade 3 Unit 5
paragraphs: Light is a form of energy that travels in straight lines called rays at an astonishing speed of 186,000 miles per second! Light can pass easily through transparent materials like clear glass, but opaque objects block light rays and cast a dark shadow.

When light rays pass from one transparent medium into another—such as from air into a glass of water—the light changes speed and bends. Scientists call this bending of light refraction. Convex lenses in eyeglasses and telescopes use refraction to focus light!

Unlike light, which can travel through empty space, sound requires a medium (solid, liquid, or gas) to travel. Every sound begins with a back-and-forth vibration. Fast vibrations produce a high-pitched sound, while slow vibrations produce a low-pitched sound.
readingPassage.audioSummary: Discover how light rays reflect and refract, and how vibrations create high and low sound waves.

paragraphs: At the center of our solar system shines the Sun, a medium-sized star whose immense gravity holds eight planets in elliptical orbits. The four inner planets—Mercury, Venus, Earth, and Mars—are rocky terrestrial planets closest to the Sun.

Beyond the asteroid belt orbit the four huge outer gas giants: Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune. Gravity is the invisible force of attraction between all objects with mass. The more mass an object has, the stronger its gravitational pull!

Our entire solar system is just one tiny part of the Milky Way, a spiral galaxy containing billions of stars. Beyond the Milky Way lie billions of other galaxies, such as our neighbor, the Andromeda Galaxy!

readingPassage.title: Native Americans of the Southwest and the Caddo of Texas
readingPassage.authorOrSource: Native American Stories • Bluebonnet Grade 3 Unit 7
paragraphs: Across North America, Native American nations developed ingenious ways of living from the land. In the dry Southwest, Pueblo peoples built multi-story villages out of sun-dried adobe clay bricks and dug irrigation canals to water fields of corn, beans, and squash.

In the fertile piney woods and river valleys of East Texas lived the Caddo nation. The Caddo were skilled farmers, potters, and traders who lived in tall, beehive-shaped grass houses framed with sturdy wooden poles.
The Caddo formed a peaceful confederacy called the Hasinai. Their word for 'friends' or 'allies' was Tejas—which Spanish explorers later used to name the state of Texas!

readingPassage.title: Explorers of the Southwest and the Search for the Northwest Passage
readingPassage.authorOrSource: The Age of Exploration • Bluebonnet Grade 3 Unit 8
paragraphs: In the 1500s and 1600s, European explorers sailed across the Atlantic Ocean searching for new trade routes to Asia and riches in the Americas. Spanish explorers such as Juan Ponce de León explored Florida, while Hernando de Soto led the first European expedition to cross the Mississippi River.

In 1540, Francisco Vásquez de Coronado led an expedition across the American Southwest, becoming the first Europeans to see the Grand Canyon and marching across the flat plains of the Texas Panhandle (the Llano Estacado).

Meanwhile, northern explorers—including John Cabot for England, Henry Hudson for the Dutch and English, and Samuel de Champlain for France—searched the icy waters of North America for a waterway to Asia called the Northwest Passage.

readingPassage.title: From Jamestown and Plymouth to the Thirteen Colonies
readingPassage.authorOrSource: Living in Colonial America • Bluebonnet Grade 3 Unit 9
paragraphs: In 1607, English settlers founded Jamestown in Virginia, the first permanent English colony in North America. Thirteen years later, in 1620, the Pilgrims sailed aboard the Mayflower to Plymouth, Massachusetts, signing the Mayflower Compact—an agreement for self-government.

Over time, thirteen English colonies developed across three distinct regions. The New England Colonies had rocky soil and cold winters, so colonists built ships, fished, and traded timber. The Middle Colonies—like Pennsylvania, founded by William Penn and the Quakers—grew so much wheat and grain they were called the 'Breadbasket Colonies.' The Southern Colonies had warm climates and long growing seasons for large farms.
By the 1770s, colonists protested British taxes made without colonial representation in Parliament, leading to the Boston Tea Party and the road to American independence!
readingPassage.audioSummary: Explore Jamestown, Plymouth, the New England, Middle, and Southern Colonies, and the Road to Revolution.

paragraphs: Born in New Orleans from a rich blend of African and European musical traditions, blues, and ragtime, jazz is a uniquely American art form celebrated around the world. A hallmark of jazz is improvisation—when musicians invent fresh melodies on the spot while performing together!

During the 1920s and 1930s, jazz became the heartbeat of the Harlem Renaissance in New York City, where writers like Langston Hughes and musicians like trumpeter Louis Armstrong, singer Billie Holiday, and bandleader Duke Ellington transformed American culture.
Later, musicians like Tito Puente blended Afro-Cuban percussion—such as timbales, bongos, and conga drums—with jazz harmonies to create lively Latin jazz and mambo rhythms!

workedExample.title: Read–Draw–Write: Equal Groups to Multiplication
workedExample.problem: Caroline, Brian, and Marta share a box of chocolates. They each get 4 chocolates. How many chocolates are there in all?
steps: Step 1 (Read): There are 3 friends (groups), and each friend gets 4 chocolates (size of each group).
Step 2 (Draw): Draw 3 circles (groups) with 4 dots in each, or a rectangular array with 3 rows of 4.
Step 3 (Write Repeated Addition): 4 + 4 + 4 = 12.
Step 4 (Write Multiplication Equation): 3 groups of four = 3 × 4 = 12 chocolates.
workedExample.solution: 3 × 4 = 12 chocolates in all.

hints: Count how many 3s are being added together. That is the number of groups!

Greetings! Rattenborough, the famous explorer and animal expert, here! Scientists classify—or sort—animals into groups based on shared characteristics so we can understand how living things are related.

One of the most important ways taxonomists classify animals is by asking: Does this animal have a backbone? Animals with a backbone are called vertebrates. Animals without a backbone, such as insects, spiders, crabs, and jellyfish, are called invertebrates. In fact, more than 95 percent of all animal species on Earth are invertebrates!

Scientists further classify vertebrates into five main groups: fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds, and mammals. Fish, amphibians, and reptiles are cold-blooded—their body temperature changes with their surroundings. Birds and mammals are warm-blooded—their bodies maintain a constant internal temperature whether it is snowy or hot outside!

Your skeletal system is made up of more than 200 bones that give your body its strong shape and protect vital organs. Your skull protects your brain like a helmet, and your rib cage shields your heart and lungs.

Light is a form of energy that travels in straight lines called rays at an astonishing speed of 186,000 miles per second! Light can pass easily through transparent materials like clear glass, but opaque objects block light rays and cast a dark shadow.

When light rays pass from one transparent medium into another—such as from air into a glass of water—the light changes speed and bends. Scientists call this bending of light refraction. Convex lenses in eyeglasses and telescopes use refraction to focus light!

Across North America, Native American nations developed ingenious ways of living from the land. In the dry Southwest, Pueblo peoples built multi-story villages out of sun-dried adobe clay bricks and dug irrigation canals to water fields of corn, beans, and squash.

In the 1500s and 1600s, European explorers sailed across the Atlantic Ocean searching for new trade routes to Asia and riches in the Americas. Spanish explorers such as Juan Ponce de León explored Florida, while Hernando de Soto led the first European expedition to cross the Mississippi River.

In 1540, Francisco Vásquez de Coronado led an expedition across the American Southwest, becoming the first Europeans to see the Grand Canyon and marching across the flat plains of the Texas Panhandle (the Llano Estacado).

Meanwhile, northern explorers—including John Cabot for England, Henry Hudson for the Dutch and English, and Samuel de Champlain for France—searched the icy waters of North America for a waterway to Asia called the Northwest Passage.

questions.passageExcerpt:
In 1607, English settlers founded Jamestown in Virginia, the first permanent English colony in North America. Thirteen years later, in 1620, the Pilgrims sailed aboard the Mayflower to Plymouth, Massachusetts, signing the Mayflower Compact—an agreement for self-government.

Over time, thirteen English colonies developed across three distinct regions. The New England Colonies had rocky soil and cold winters, so colonists built ships, fished, and traded timber. The Middle Colonies—like Pennsylvania, founded by William Penn and the Quakers—grew so much wheat and grain they were called the 'Breadbasket Colonies.' The Southern Colonies had warm climates and long growing seasons for large farms.

By the 1770s, colonists protested British taxes made without colonial representation in Parliament, leading to the Boston Tea Party and the road to American independence!

Born in New Orleans from a rich blend of African and European musical traditions, blues, and ragtime, jazz is a uniquely American art form celebrated around the world. A hallmark of jazz is improvisation—when musicians invent fresh melodies on the spot while performing together!

During the 1920s and 1930s, jazz became the heartbeat of the Harlem Renaissance in New York City, where writers like Langston Hughes and musicians like trumpeter Louis Armstrong, singer Billie Holiday, and bandleader Duke Ellington transformed American culture.

Later, musicians like Tito Puente blended Afro-Cuban percussion—such as timbales, bongos, and conga drums—with jazz harmonies to create lively Latin jazz and mambo rhythms!
